title: Dyke–Davidoff–Masson syndrome in a Nigerian
case_prompt:
A 27-year-old woman presented with her father for evaluation of recurrent seizures and poor scholastic performance. She was born at term without complications. At age 2 years, she experienced a febrile seizure characterized by focal clonic movements of the left side that evolved to a bilateral convulsion and was followed by three days of unconsciousness. On discharge, she had residual left hemiparesis. Approximately 15 years ago, she developed recurrent generalized tonic–clonic seizures. She demonstrated impaired cognition and poor academic performance, preventing completion of secondary education. Her medication history included trials of phenobarbital, carbamazepine, and phenytoin with persistent poor seizure control and gingival hyperplasia.

On examination, her weight was 43.7 kg and height 1.56 m (BMI 17.9 kg/m²). Her score on Raven’s Standard Progressive Matrices was 11/60 (below the 5th percentile). Neurologically, she had left facial hemiatrophy, left hemibody atrophy, and spastic hemiparesis (4/5 strength in left upper and lower limbs) with a left extensor plantar response. The remainder of the examination was normal. Based on these findings, Rasmussen encephalitis was suspected, and cranial magnetic resonance imaging and electroencephalography were requested.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Rasmussen encephalitis was considered — “In Rasmussen's syndrome, the calvarial changes are not found.”
2. Todd’s paralysis was considered — “benign etiologies such as Todd's paralysis … are easily identifiable”
3. Metabolic electrolyte abnormalities were considered — “metabolic etiologies such as glucose, sodium, potassium, calcium, and magnesium abnormalities are easily identifiable”
4. Structural lesions including neoplasms, abscesses, ADEM, malformations, trauma, and infarctions were considered — “structural lesions such as neoplasms, intracerebral abscesses, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, developmental brain malformations, and signs of trauma and vascular disorders … should be excluded”
5. Hemiconvulsion-hemiplegia-epilepsy (HHE) syndrome was considered — “generalized tonic-clonic seizures after hemiconvulsions … are less typical of HHE syndrome … long latency … between the acute encephalopathy and the onset of epilepsy (typically 2 months to 2 years in HHE)”
6. Sturge–Weber syndrome was considered — “In Sturge–Weber syndrome, brain imaging shows enhancing pial angiomas and cortical calcifications”
7. Basal ganglia germinoma was considered — “brain imaging reveals cystic areas, focal hemorrhages, and mild surrounding edema along with calvarial changes”
8. Silver–Russell syndrome was considered — “Silver–Russell syndrome … normal intelligence”
9. Fishman syndrome (encephalocraniocutaneous lipomatosis) was considered — “Neuroimaging, however, shows a calcified cortex and hemiatrophy”
10. Linear nevus sebaceous syndrome was considered — “Linear nevus sebaceous syndrome … is characterized by a typical facial nevus, mental retardation, recurrent seizures, and hemimegaencephaly”
11. Dyke–Davidoff–Masson syndrome was concluded — “The findings of cerebral hemiatrophy, calvarial thickening, and hyperpneumatization of the frontal sinuses on MRI … are the diagnostic criteria for DDMS in this case.”
